problems.description: Replaces the seeded REST/JSON API with a hand-rolled SOAP service — envelope and fault serialization built via f-string concatenation + ElementTree rather than a SOAP library — and collapses four typed routes into a single monolithic /tasks dispatcher, which is more fragile and harder to extend than the per-route pattern it replaced.
ET.fromstring() parses an unauthenticated POST body; xml.etree.ElementTree is susceptible to billion-laughs entity expansion, so the SOAP endpoint should use defusedxml.
Type hints on get_task/update_task (dict | None, str | None) that existed in the baseline were stripped, a step backwards in type safety on otherwise-unchanged DB functions.
init_db() moved from the __main__ guard to module import time, creating an import-time side effect (DB initialization on every import).

The 0.73 convention score (8 violations) is not attributable to this commit: 6 violations are in files outside the diff (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py — pre-existing), and the app.py/test_app.py class-naming violations appear to be false positives since the AST reports +0 classes added.

strengths: DB seam preserved — get_db/create_task/get_tasks/get_task/update_task reused unchanged; only the transport layer was rewritten.
All dynamic strings in generated XML are escaped via xml.sax.saxutils.escape, preventing XML injection in titles/status.
Both SOAP 1.1 and SOAP 1.2 envelope namespaces are handled, and faults map to correct HTTP status codes (400/404).
Style within the touched files is consistent (snake_case helpers, UPPER_CASE module constants, section markers), and a test file was added.
commit_reviews.summary: Session 1 trades a clean, typed REST baseline for a hand-rolled SOAP endpoint that keeps the DB seam intact but removes type hints, adds import-time side effects, and exposes an unguarded XML parser — worse on architectural fit and convention than what it replaced.

problems.description: Generated JWTs carry no expiry claim (payload is only sub/username), so tokens never expire; combined with the hardcoded 'insecure-dev-secret' fallback for SECRET_KEY, a leaked token or default secret grants indefinite access.
SECRET_KEY defaults to 'insecure-dev-secret' when the environment variable is absent; the fallback should fail fast or generate a random key rather than silently shipping a known secret.

Auth is introduced as REST endpoints (POST /auth/register, /auth/login) inside what was a single-endpoint SOAP service, mixing protocols; workable but slightly at odds with the documented SOAP-only surface, and owner_id is now threaded through every handler/helper, which drives the measured cognitive complexity +20.
Schema migration (PRAGMA-driven ALTER TABLE) lives inline inside init_db rather than a dedicated migration path; acceptable for this size but will not scale to subsequent schema changes.

strengths: Passwords are hashed with werkzeug generate_password_hash/check_password_hash, never stored in plaintext.
Per-owner scoping is applied at the query layer for list/get/update, giving real tenant isolation rather than client-side filtering.
The owner_id migration is backward compatible — pre-existing task rows keep a NULL owner and are not disturbed.

New code follows existing repo conventions: snake_case helpers, get_db() context-manager usage, dict(row) return shape, and the module docstring style, with no new convention violations introduced by the added lines.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, convention-consistent auth feature — proper hashing and per-owner data scoping — slightly marred by non-expiring tokens and a hardcoded dev secret fallback.

problems.description: New runtime dependency on `celery` (tasks.py, celery_config.py) is not recorded in requirements.txt or any manifest — only 2 files were added (AST: +2 files), so the app import path now breaks on environments without celery installed.
Async notification has no retry/error handling and silently drops if no Celery worker consumes the `email` queue; the mock prints to console, so a real integration is not enforced.

`get_user()` returns the full row via `SELECT *`, including `password_hash`, when only email/username are needed — a least-privilege smell (hash is not exposed to clients but is fetched into the notification path).
Silently fabricates fallback addresses like `{username}@example.com` and persists them into the users table; if a real mailer is wired later these would be sent to non-owned addresses.
Notification path is tested only via mocked `send_notification_email`; the actual `.delay()` enqueue, task_routes queue routing (`email`), and worker execution are never exercised.

Mechanical convention score 0.73 (8 violations) overcounts real issues: `celery_config.py` lowercase module attrs (broker_url/result_backend) are Celery's own convention, and the PascalCase/snake_case flags point at files/functions that add no classes or functions (analyzer false positives); one flag references repositories.py, which is not touched by this commit.

strengths: Trigger logic correctly fires only on the non-completed→completed transition and is guarded against re-notification on already-completed tasks, with 5 targeted tests covering custom email, other statuses, and title-only updates.
Incremental DB migration for pre-existing user tables is done properly, guarded by PRAGMA schema introspection with a default on new tables.
Async decoupling via Celery `.delay()` keeps the SOAP request path fast, with a dedicated `email` queue via task_routes and broker/backend config overridable by env vars.
Follows the app's existing flat-module, type-hinted style (get_user mirrors get_task/current_user) and the repo's monkeypatch-based test conventions.
SonarQube reports zero new bugs, zero smells, and zero duplication; cognitive complexity +10 is modest for the added notification logic.
commit_reviews.summary: Clean, well-tested async integration that fits the app's existing flat-module architecture and handles the completed-transition edge cases correctly, though it introduces an undeclared celery dependency and its mechanical convention score (0.73) is inflated by analyzer false positives and Celery-conventional lowercase config.

problems.description: task_repo and user_repo are instantiated as module-level singletons at import time (TaskRepository(get_db)), creating global state that tests or re-configuration must work around; a lazy factory or per-request construction would avoid import-time coupling.

repositories.py introduces module-level constants that do not use UPPER_CASE (per measurement), and the new classes in the touched files trip the PascalCase check — the 0.73 convention score's repo-wide violations are mostly in untouched files, but the new module adds at least one.

Repository method names (create, all, get, update) are generic; the domain context the removed functions carried (create_task, get_tasks, get_task) now lives only at call sites, slightly reducing readability.

strengths: Clean layering: raw SQL moved out of the SOAP/controller layer into TaskRepository/UserRepository, improving separation of concerns.
Consolidated duplicated user queries (create_user, authenticate, get_user, and current_user's inline lookup) into a single UserRepository.
Schema creation and the idempotent column-migration logic centralized into create_schema, preserving the migration behavior for pre-existing tables.
Removed now-unused imports (datetime, werkzeug password helpers), tightening the import surface.
SonarQube delta is clean: +0 bugs, +0 smells, +0.0% duplications.
commit_reviews.summary: Genuine improvement — SQL extracted into a repository layer with zero new bugs or smells — though the 0.73 convention score reflects repo-wide violations concentrated in untouched files (celery_config.py, tasks.py, test_app.py) rather than this diff, so the commit's own compliance is better than the score suggests.

compounding_issues: Session 3's Celery integration accreted the monolith to ~270 lines of app.py; session 4 had to pay that down via the Repository pattern rather than building new features
Session 2's default SECRET_KEY ('dev-secret-key', 14 bytes) persisted into the final build and trips an InsecureKeyLengthWarning on every JWT decode
Rate-limit storage hardcodes redis://localhost:6379, coupling the app to Redis availability rather than reading it from the environment
key_decisions: Extract repositories/ package (base/task/user_repository.py) in Session 4, removing direct SQLite access from routes and providing the clean layering Session 5 built on
Adopt Celery (celery_config.py) in Session 3 for async email notifications, decoupling status-change side effects from the request lifecycle
Add JWT auth with a User model in Session 2 (register/login), establishing identity before per-user rate limiting was introduced in Session 5
Maintain a growing pytest suite from Session 1 onward (124→321 lines), keeping every session's additions guarded — 36/36 tests pass at the final commit
Choose Flask-Limiter with Redis for per-user rate limits plus pagination in Session 5 as the cross-cutting capstone
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved across the five sessions with a textbook 'build-then-pay-down' arc. Session 1 produced a clean greenfield API with tests (128 LOC app, 124 LOC tests); Session 2 cleanly layered JWT auth; Session 3 added Celery integration but the single file grew to ~270 lines. Session 4 was the pivotal refactor — extracting the Repository pattern cut app.py from 270 to 165 lines and removed direct SQLite from routes — so Session 5's cross-cutting work (rate limiting, pagination, plus repository additions) landed on a clean base, ending at 214 app + 321 test lines with all 36 tests passing. The arc shows deliberate accumulation, a mid-story structural correction, and extension on the corrected architecture; the only softening is that Session 5 was the heaviest lift (ran to the full 600s budget, highest token/cost spend), suggesting the cross-cutting scope was ambitious even on the refactored base.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, well-sequenced story whose session themes map to a natural software lifecycle, capped by a mid-story Repository refactor that prevented feature accumulation from becoming technical debt.
